body_markdown:
Hemingway was fond of referring to 1920s Paris as “a moveable feast” for the literary set. For car people, that phrase applies to the area around the Monterey Peninsula during Car Week. The Pebble Beach Concours, the auctions, and events like Motorlux and The Quail are the obvious places to look at great cars, but in my 20-plus years of attending Monterey Car Week, I’ve found that the really interesting/weird stuff often hides in plain sight, street parked by car week attendees, or in residential neighborhoods, still in daily use and enjoying the metal-friendly environment of California. Here are a few of my random favorites from this year. The years are my best guess.


### 1975 Cadillac Coupe de Ville


Rob Sass


A two-door car that clocks in at almost 20-feet in length and 5200 pounds is impressive, even in the EV era. But this behemoth was powered by a massive 500-cubic inch V-8 that made, wait for it, 190 horsepower. Peak Malaise Era numbers right there. I took a wrong turn in Monterey looking for a Vietnamese restaurant, and there it was, resplendent in what appeared to be its original Bombay Yellow, with the proper wheel covers and bright white landau vinyl roof and a parking ticket. The car was simply gorgeous. Back in the day, Potamkin Cadillac in NYC practically sold these things in bulk. Whoever drives this in California with its 9-mpg fuel economy and $6 per gallon gas prices should get some kind of award.


### 1981 BMW Alpina B9 3.5


Rob Sass


Alpina was (and is) to BMW what AMG was to Mercedes-Benz. Now that the company has been similarly absorbed, maybe there will be more attention directed to the pre-merger cars like this beauty. Any E24 BMW 6-series coupe is a pretty car, and this one, with its small Euro bumpers and grey/green metallic paint with the classic Alpina side stripes is a serious looker. The crazy striped Recaro buckets add immeasurably to the appeal of a car that went like an M6 before the M6 was a thing, (courtesty of an Alpina-tuned 245-hp 3.5-liter six).


### 1967 Mercedes-Benz 250 SE Coupe


Rob Sass


Rob Sass


A Mercedes coupe isn’t the most common choice of car to restomod, but this car looked positively incandescent street parked on Cannery Row on Friday night where it would have won Best in Show had there been such an award for street parked cars during Car Week. It wasn’t just the gorgeous smoky silver paint and bright trim, but the car’s stance on modern BBS wheels and low-profile tires worked surprisingly well. Everyone was snapping photos of the car. The owner got in just after I took this shot, I complemented him on his good taste, he nodded knowingly, and drove off.


### Three RADwood-Era Toyotas


Rob Sass


Rob Sass


Rob Sass


In a rare three-for-one, I couldn’t help snapping these insanely rust-free vintage, blue-collar Toyotas. The white sedan is, believe it or not, a first-generation Camry (1981 or so), an example of which I haven’t seen since the George H.W. Bush presidency. While there’s no shortage of bird droppings on it, and there’s a brick/wheel chock present indicating at the very least hand-brake failure, it does have a current registration and somehow escaped Cash for Clunkers. The silver 4Runner is a 1991 or 1992 I think and was also not blighted by body rot. When you can find these for sale, even with close to 300,000 miles, these amazing rigs still bring around $7000. The impossibly clean red Tacoma from about 1999 was in classic California spec—no terminal frame rust, a short cab and two-wheel-drive.


### 1978 Volkswagen Scirocco


Rob Sass


The[Scirocco](https://www.hagerty.com/valuation-tools/search?q=volkswagen+scirocco) was the car that essentially replaced the[Karmann Ghia](https://www.hagerty.com/valuation-tools/search?q=volkswagen+karmann+ghia) . Instead of a Beetle in an Italian suit, it was a MK I Golf in an Italian suit, this time by the immortal Giorgetto Giugiaro. A masterpiece in subtle wedge design, these were fun, tossable little cars. Sadly, most are gone. It’s incredibly rare to see one in the wild, even one with some patina like this one in its faded silver paint. The orange badging, stripes, and front air dam might mark this as some kind of special edition, or just one with a bunch of dealer add-ons. The answer to that might be lost to history, but this one was still doing its thing on the streets of Monterey.


### 1962 Lincoln Continental


Rob Sass


It doesn’t get much more iconic American than this. The early ’60s[Continental](https://www.hagerty.com/valuation-tools/search?q=1962+lincoln+continental) was peak mid-century modern luxury, and quite honestly, I didn’t see anyone in Monterey having an appreciably better time than these five guys cruising in a bagged, ivory Continental convertible with wide whites. In an ever-expanding sea of influencers, it was refreshing to see some unimpeachably old-school, authentic badassery in Monterey.


### 1970 Chevrolet K5 Blazer


Rob Sass


The K5[Blazer](https://www.hagerty.com/valuation-tools/search?q=1970+blazer) is maybe one of the best-loved, an most underrated of the early crop of SUVs. Once again, GM was late to the party and found itself playing catch-up to the likes International Harvester’s[Scout](https://www.hagerty.com/valuation-tools/search?q=1967+scout) and Ford’s[Bronco](https://www.hagerty.com/valuation-tools/search?q=1967+bronco) . At least the Blazer was really good. Not surprising, since it was based on the C/K pickup series. This one was beautifully restored in what appears to be the original Blazer shade of Dark Blue Green standing out in a sea of grey Japanese and Korean sedans like a velociraptor at the Westminster Kennel Club Dog Show.


### 2009 Saab 9-3X Aero SportCombi XWD


Rob Sass


To the untrained eye, this car might be easily dismissable as just another Subaru Outback, but in reality it was one of the rarer cars on the streets of Monterey. This turbocharged AWD six-speed manual wagon is one of a mere handful built by Saab before it shut down car production in 2011. Even as high-mileage orphans, long-roof fanatics will still pay around $10,000 for one of these. This one looked like a very nice survivor.


### 1968 Shelby GT350 Convertible


Rob Sass


I’m embarrassed to admit, but the first time that I attended Monterey Car Week was some time in the late 1980s. Back then, the Pebble Beach Concours and an auction run by Rick Cole at the Portola hotel was pretty much all there was, and ratty unrestored versions of cars like this were everywhere. Now, they’re too valuable to risk street parking, unless you’re this owner who popped in for dinner on Cannery Row. I’m no Shelby expert, but this one appears slightly restomodded with its modern 17” wheels. Still, it had quite the presence in black/white, and it sounded fantastic.


### 1964 Volkswagen Beetle


Rob Sass


At first glance, there’s nothing terribly remarkable about an air-cooled VW Beetle. After all, they sold an incredible 569,000 of these in the U.S. in 1970 alone. In 2026, however, a street parked, unrestored, rust-free Beetle that appears to be a daily driver is an incredibly rare sight. I saw this car trundling around Monterey during the course of the week with an octogenarian driver that could well have been the original owner. By sheer happenstance, I caught it parked in a residential neighborhood of Seaside while in futile search of a parking place for Concours d’Lemons. It looked fantastic with its faded ivory paint, patinated wheels, and vintage decals. Long may it continue to provide basic transportation to someone.


### 1986 Suzuki Samurai


Rob Sass


The[Suzuki Samurai](https://www.hagerty.com/valuation-tools/search?q=suzuki+samurai) was a sub-Jeep sized 4X4 sold in the U.S. from 1985 to 1995. Known to the rest of the world as the Jimny, it continues to be sold nearly everywhere except for here. Lightweight and made with thin sheetmetal, most Samurais disappeared from U.S. roads decades ago. But not this beaut on its original white spoker wheels. It was another only-in-California sighting of a once common car that is now exceedingly rare.


### 1963 Facel Vega Facel III


Rob Sass


It’s not every day that you see a car that bankrupted a company. The Facellia, the little brother to the Chrysler Hemi-powered Facel Vega, was supposed to sell in large numbers but was a giant dud owing to its unreliable twin-cam engine. This car, the identical Facel III was actually powered by a reliable 1.8-liter Volvo engine, but the damage had already been done and the whole company went down the tubes. I saw this ultra-rare French car all over Monterey, both parked in one of the municipal garages downtown and parked at Concours d’Lemons.


### 1986 Lincoln MK VII LSC


Rob Sass


This Fox platform beauty was the closest that Dearborn came to building a European style luxury GT to compete with BMW and Mercedes. With leather bucket seats, relatively taut suspension (with air springs) and a fuel-injected 5.0-liter V-8, it was a decent performer, even if the handling from its live rear axle wasn’t quite up to German standards. I honestly can’t remember the last time I saw one of these cars anywhere. This grey one had the looks of a low-mileage, all original car. I loved it.


### 1969 Alfa Romeo Duetto


Rob Sass


The little[Alfa Spider](https://www.hagerty.com/valuation-tools/alfa_romeo/giulia/1966/1966-alfa_romeo-giulia-duetto_spider?id=aCn1I000000Cyn9SAC) might be one of the most iconic cars of the 1960s because of its on-screen presence in the classic film *The Graduate* . This one’s rounded “boat tail” and scooped headlights that lack glass covers I believe mark this as a 1969 model year. It was part of the massive presence of classics on Cannery Row Friday night.
